article.title: Fitzpatrick Skin Type Test: 5-Question Quiz and Results
article.meta_description: Take a quick Fitzpatrick skin type test, see what types I to VI mean, and learn how it differs from skin tone and undertone for makeup and style.
article.h1: Fitzpatrick Skin Type Test: A 5-Question Self-Quiz (Types I to VI)
article.body_html:
A Fitzpatrick skin type test sorts you into one of six types, I to VI, based on how your skin usually reacts to sun: whether it burns, whether it tans, and how deeply. The quiz below takes about two minutes and gives you a rough self-estimate. It is our own simplified version, not the questionnaire a professional would use, and it is a different thing from your skin tone or undertone.

Fitzpatrick skin type test: the short answer

What the scale is

Dermatologist Thomas Fitzpatrick developed the scale in the 1970s to describe how different skin responds to sunlight. Type I burns very easily and barely tans. Type VI is deeply pigmented and very rarely burns. Types II to V sit in between.

What this quiz can and can't tell you

It can give you a starting estimate of your sun reactivity and clear up the confusion between sun reaction, skin depth and undertone. It can't give you an official classification. If an exact type matters for your situation, ask a qualified professional.

What the Fitzpatrick scale measures (and what it doesn't)

Sun reaction: burning and tanning tendency

The scale comes down to two questions: how readily do you burn, and how readily do you tan? That is why the quiz puts those questions first and weighs them most heavily.

Why it isn't a measure of how light or dark skin looks

Two people can look similar in photos and react to sun differently, and two people who look quite different can share a type. Pigment and reaction often travel together, which is why color questions appear in quizzes, but color is only a clue.

What it doesn't tell you about your skin

Your type describes a general tendency in how skin responds to sun. It is a broad category, not a description of your individual skin today.

Before you start: how to answer fairly

  • Think about your usual reaction, not your best tan. Recall what typically happens at the start of a season, not after weeks of gradual exposure.
  • Ignore sunscreen, recent tans and one-off burns. One bad burn on a cloudy day doesn't define you. Look for the pattern.
  • Answer about your natural coloring. Skip dyed hair and colored contact lenses.

If you can't remember how your skin reacts, pick the option that matches what you've seen over several years, and consider what you know of your family's pattern.

The self-test: 5 questions

Questions 1 to 3 are about sun reaction and score 0 to 4. Questions 4 and 5 are about coloring and score 0 to 2, so reaction counts for more. Write down your five numbers and add them up at the end.

Question 1: What usually happens after your first unprotected sun exposure of a season?

  • 0: A painful burn, often with blistering or peeling
  • 1: A burn, usually followed by peeling
  • 2: A mild burn, sometimes
  • 3: I rarely burn
  • 4: I almost never burn

Question 2: Does your skin tan afterward, and how deeply?

  • 0: Never. I turn red, then return to my usual color, and may freckle
  • 1: A faint tan, with difficulty
  • 2: A gradual light-to-medium tan
  • 3: I tan easily to a moderate brown
  • 4: I tan deeply and quickly, or my skin is already deeply pigmented with little visible change

Question 3: How quickly does your face redden in the sun?

  • 0: Very quickly
  • 1: Fairly easily
  • 2: Sometimes
  • 3: Rarely
  • 4: I hardly ever notice any reddening

Question 4: What is your natural skin color in areas rarely exposed to sun?

  • 0: Very pale to fair
  • 1: Light beige, medium, or olive
  • 2: Brown to very deep brown

Question 5: What are your natural eye and hair colors?

  • 0: Red, blond or light brown hair, with blue, green, gray or light hazel eyes
  • 1: Medium to dark brown hair, with hazel or brown eyes
  • 2: Black or near-black hair, with very dark brown eyes

If your coloring is mixed, such as dark hair with light eyes, simply pick the closest match.

How to add up your answers

Total score (0 to 16)Approximate type
0 to 2Type I
3 to 5Type II
6 to 8Type III
9 to 11Type IV
12 to 14Type V
15 to 16Type VI

These bands are our own simplification for organizing your answers, not a validated scoring system. Read the result as a ballpark, and if your total sits near a boundary, treat it as a tie between two types.

Your result: Fitzpatrick types I to VI at a glance

Types I and II: burn easily, tan little

Type I typically burns every time and doesn't tan. Type II burns easily and tans minimally. Both are often associated with very fair skin and light eyes or hair, though not always.

Types III and IV: sometimes burn, tan gradually

Type III may burn at first, then tans to a light brown. Type IV burns only a little and tans readily to a moderate brown. These two types cover a wide range of looks, including many medium and olive complexions.

Types V and VI: rarely burn, tan deeply or have deeply pigmented skin

Type V rarely burns and tans darkly. Type VI very rarely burns and has deeply pigmented skin. Burning is less common for these types but still possible, so sun protection still applies.

If you land between two types

That is common. Many people sit on a border such as II/III or IV/V. Note both and don't force a single answer.

Why a self-test can be off

Memory, past tans and sunscreen habits skew answers

If you always wear sunscreen, you may never have seen your skin's unprotected reaction. If you've tanned for years, your recent history may not reflect your natural response.

Why the scale can feel too broad for deeper skin tones

Many people with deeper skin feel the scale lumps them into just two types, V and VI, despite a wide range of depth and undertone. That criticism is fair. The scale was built around sun reaction, not to describe the full variety of skin color. Reddening can also be harder to see on deeper skin, which can make Question 3 tricky; lean on Questions 1 and 2 if so.

Why a quiz is only a rough guide

A professional can consider your history and family background in person. Five questions can't, so use your result as an estimate.

Fitzpatrick type vs skin tone vs undertone

Three different questions

  • Fitzpatrick type: how your skin reacts to sun.
  • Skin depth (tone): how light or deep your skin looks.
  • Undertone: the cool, warm, neutral or olive cast beneath the surface.

Why the same type can need different foundation shades

Two people who are both Type III could be a light neutral and a medium warm in foundation terms. The scale says nothing about depth or undertone, so it can't pick a shade for you.

Which to use for what

For makeup shades and clothing colors, depth and undertone are the useful measures. Our guide to finding your skin tone and depth walks through it, and the undertone tests are a quick way to check the cool-versus-warm question.

Sun safety: what your type does and doesn't mean

Every type needs sun protection

A higher number doesn't mean you can skip sunscreen, shade or protective clothing. Skin of every type is affected by sun exposure.

Your type is only a sun-reaction category

The Fitzpatrick scale is a general grouping. Use it for context, not as a tool for assessing your own skin.

Where to take real questions

AI feedback, including anything from FitCheck AI, is not medical advice, so please see a dermatologist or doctor about any skin concern. Choices about tanning or skin procedures are also best made with a qualified professional.

Using your results for style and makeup

Skip Fitzpatrick for shade matching

Use the quiz to understand your sun reactivity, then set it aside for beauty decisions. Foundation, blush and clothing colors depend on depth and undertone.

Simple starting points once you know your tone

  • Cool undertone: try berry or rosy lip colors, and clothing in navy, emerald or cool gray. For example, a navy blazer with a white tee and gray trousers.
  • Warm undertone: try peach or terracotta blush, and clothing in olive, camel or rust. For example, an olive overshirt over a cream tee with tan chinos.
  • Neutral or olive undertone: you can often wear both families. Hold a fabric near your face in daylight and see whether your skin looks fresh or dull.

For makeup choices based on your features, the makeup guide for your face is a good next step.

Where FitCheck AI can fit in (and where it can't)

What the live skin analysis gives you

FitCheck AI's live skin analysis uses the camera to give an AI skin overview with cosmetic beauty suggestions. Think of it as a second opinion on the style side, a starting point for ideas.

What it doesn't do

It does not assign a Fitzpatrick type, so this quiz and the app answer different questions. The app's feedback is an AI opinion focused on cosmetic suggestions.

Photo tips

For makeup and hair, face natural light, hold the camera at eye level and avoid filters. Filters and warm indoor bulbs can change how your skin color appears.

faqs.question: Can my Fitzpatrick type change over time?
faqs.answer: The type describes your skin's typical tendency and is generally treated as stable. Your coloring can look different with a seasonal tan, but that doesn't usually mean you've changed type. If you're unsure, treat your result as a range between two types.

faqs.question: Is Fitzpatrick type the same as skin tone?
faqs.answer: No. Fitzpatrick type is about how your skin reacts to sun, skin tone describes how light or deep your skin looks, and undertone describes its cool, warm or neutral cast. They often overlap, but they answer different questions.

faqs.question: Can I use my Fitzpatrick type to choose foundation?
faqs.answer: Not reliably. People of the same type can need very different shades because depth and undertone vary within each type. Try swatches along your jaw and neck in natural daylight instead.

faqs.question: Does a higher number mean I don't need sunscreen?
faqs.answer: No. Types V and VI burn less often, but sun protection still matters for every type.

faqs.question: Can an app tell me my Fitzpatrick type?
faqs.answer: FitCheck AI does not assign a Fitzpatrick type. Its live skin analysis offers an AI skin overview with cosmetic beauty suggestions.

review.notes:
The article gives a usable, honest self-quiz. It states that the scoring bands are its own simplification and not a validated tool, and it explains Fitzpatrick type vs skin depth vs undertone clearly. The scoring arithmetic is consistent (max 12 + 4 = 16, with bands covering 0-16). App claims match APP_FACTS: live skin analysis is described as cosmetic and not medical, the article says it does not assign a Fitzpatrick type, and Android-only availability is stated correctly. It makes no accuracy, storage or privacy claims. Medical referrals are present and appropriate, and the styling and undertone advice is sound.

Minor suggestions, not blockers:
- Q2 option 4 combines two ideas (tans deeply vs already deeply pigmented). Splitting or rewording it would be cleaner.
- A typical Type III answer set (for example 1, 2, 1, 1, 0 = 5) lands in the Type II band. The 'treat boundaries as a tie' note covers this, but the bands could be tuned.
- The article could mention that the original Fitzpatrick scale had only types I-IV and that V-VI were added later. It could also name the standard clinical questionnaire for readers who want it.
- The CTA and app section are modest and not pushy. The article is mostly informational, which suits the intent.
